sentences.text: The name Aerosteon translates to "air bone," a title derived from Greek roots.
Fossils show clear evidence of a bird-like respiratory system.
Its bones display pneumatization, meaning they contain hollow spaces and air-filled cavities.
Remains were found in 1996 within the Anacleto Formation.
The species was first described by Sereno and colleagues in a paper published in PLoS ONE in September 2008.
The holotype specimen, which serves as the basis for the species description, includes cranial bones, vertebrae, ribs, gastralia, a furcula, and various limb bones.
Analysis of the bones indicates the individual was not fully mature when it died, as shown by the incomplete fusion of its skeletal elements.
No teeth are currently known for Aerosteon because the single tooth originally assigned to the holotype was later identified as belonging to an abelisaurid.
These air sacs acted like bellows to move air through its inflexible lungs, unlike the expanding and contracting lungs of mammals.
Researchers theorize that this respiratory system originally developed to regulate body temperature and was later adapted for breathing.
A later analysis placed the Megaraptora, including Aerosteon, within the Tyrannosauroidea.
Some analyses consider Megaraptorans, including Aerosteon, as non-tyrannosauroid basal coelurosaurs.
The parent group of Aerosteon is Megaraptoridae.
Aerosteon is classified as a reptile.
Aerosteon lived during the Late Cretaceous period in Argentina.
Other data places its existence in the Campanian stage, spanning from 83.6 to 72.2 million years ago.
It is debated whether Murusraptor and Aerosteon are distinct genera, as they are nearly identical in skull and vertebrae structure but differ in ilium proportions and tooth morphology.
